title: NEB Class 11 Physics — Rate of Heat Flow — 2024
subject: physics
topicTitle: NEB Class 11 Physics — Rate of Heat Flow — 2024
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: Define conduction, convection, and radiation, giving one example of each.
questions.solution:
**Conduction:** heat flows through a material by molecular collisions, no bulk motion — e.g. a metal spoon heating in tea.

**Convection:** heat carried by the bulk movement of fluid — e.g. hot air rising in a room.

**Radiation:** heat transferred as electromagnetic waves, needing no medium — e.g. warmth from the Sun.
questions.knowledgeNote: Solids conduct; fluids convect; everything radiates — most real situations mix at least two.

questions.question: State Fourier's law of heat conduction and explain each term.
questions.solution:
**Fourier's law:** Q/t = kA(ΔT/d).

Q/t = rate of heat flow (J/s); k = thermal conductivity of the material; A = cross-sectional area; ΔT = temperature difference between the ends; d = length along the flow.

Heat flows faster through short, fat, highly conducting bars with a steep temperature drop.
questions.knowledgeNote: k has units W/m·K — copper (~400) vs air (~0.026) explains why metals feel cold and wool feels warm.

questions.question: A metal rod 0.5 m long with cross-section 4 cm² has its ends at 100°C and 0°C. If k = 400 W/m·K, find the rate of heat flow through the rod.
questions.knowledgeNote: Steady state is assumed — the ends held at fixed temperatures so no heat accumulates in the rod.

questions.question: State Stefan's law of black-body radiation. If the absolute temperature of a body is doubled, by what factor does its radiated power increase?
questions.solution:
**Stefan's law:** the total energy radiated per unit area per second is E = σT⁴ (σ = 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W/m²K⁴).

Since E ∝ T⁴, doubling T multiplies the power by 2⁴ = **16 times**.
questions.knowledgeNote: T⁴ sensitivity is why a small rise in filament temperature makes a bulb dramatically brighter.

questions.question: Why are cooking utensils blackened at the bottom, and why do people prefer white clothes in summer?
questions.solution:
Black surfaces are the best absorbers (and emitters) of radiation: a blackened bottom **absorbs the flame's radiant heat** fastest, cooking food quicker.

White clothes **reflect** most of the Sun's radiation instead of absorbing it, keeping the wearer cooler — the same reason houses in hot regions are painted white.
questions.knowledgeNote: Good absorber = good emitter (Kirchhoff's law) — which is also why blackened utensils cool faster once off the flame.

questions.question: State Newton's law of cooling and give one practical application.
questions.solution:
**Newton's law of cooling:** the rate of loss of heat of a body is directly proportional to the temperature difference between the body and its surroundings (for small differences).

**Application:** forensic estimation of time of death from body temperature, or judging how long tea has been standing from its temperature.
questions.knowledgeNote: The law holds only for small ΔT and still air — forced draughts (a fan on hot tea) cool faster than it predicts.
